payload.previous_feedback: Previous vetter reason: The argument is correct and complete: it uses the defining property of floor to show that assuming x >= floor(x)+1 contradicts maximality of floor(x). The conclusion x < floor(x)+1 follows directly, with no semantic drift and no dependency issues.
payload.previous_proof_nl: Let x be any real number, and set m = floor(x). By the definition of the floor function, m is an integer and m <= x, and moreover m is the greatest integer with this property. Suppose for contradiction that x >= m + 1. Then m + 1 is also an integer, and m + 1 <= x. This contradicts the maximality of m, since m + 1 > m is an integer still not exceeding x. Therefore x < m + 1. Since m = floor(x), we obtain x < floor(x) + 1. Because x was arbitrary, the statement holds for every real number x.

result_payload.addressed_previous_feedback: The previous feedback indicated the argument was already correct and complete. This revision preserves the same maximality-of-floor argument and states it explicitly in a fully rigorous contradiction form.
result_payload.proof_nl: Let x be any real number, and set m = floor(x). By the defining property of the floor function, m is an integer, m <= x, and m is the greatest integer with this property. Suppose for contradiction that x >= m + 1. Then m + 1 is an integer and also m + 1 <= x. But this contradicts the maximality of m, since m + 1 > m is a larger integer still not exceeding x. Hence the assumption is impossible, so x < m + 1. Substituting m = floor(x), we obtain x < floor(x) + 1. Because x was arbitrary, the statement holds for every real number x.
result_payload.proof_summary: Fix x and let m = floor(x). If x were at least m+1, then m+1 would be an integer not exceeding x, contradicting that m is the greatest integer <= x. Therefore x < floor(x)+1 for all real x.
